#3747. The hunt for World of Warcraft: Forever secrets continue with the discovery of an elusive pet

The search for secrets in World of Warcraft: Forever continues ever onwards, with a new breakthrough coming to light in recent days. The latest discovery? An elusive new cat that can be tamed by hunters in one of the game's new zones.

The cat's name is Ta'Shkal, and they can be found on Mount Hyjal. An endgame levelling zone, players will have to reach at least level 57 in order to safely make their way up there and recruit this new pet.

The way you do so is relatively simple. You need to find a small corrupted cat figuring within the Felblood Scar region of Mount Hyjal. Once you've found that, you then need to travel up to a hidden lantern south of the Mourning's Rest area. With the figurine in your bags, you'll be able to interact with the lantern, spawning the cat for you to tame (granted you're playing a hunter).

So what's the big deal about this cat? Well, aside from the fact it's got a strange colour scheme of green fur with orange stripes, the cat also has a base attack speed of 1.0. This means it'll attack once every second, which is pretty fast and allows for greater damage output from your pet. This inherently makes the pet valuable for endgame hunter players, who are looking to improve their performance in PvE and PvP.

This is not the only secret discovered by World of Warcraft: Forever sleuths. Last week, they pieced together a hidden quest chain that leads to two special swords. As of writing, only one has been found, though progress continues in pursuit of the second.

The game has been out for just over two weeks now, and continues to prove popular among new and returning players. It's the biggest launch in the series' history, and has gone down well with people so far. Even if it has recently suffered its first controversy with a now-fixed gold exploit.

#3746. Vote now for 2026's RPS 100: Reader Edition

For the past six years, the team at RPS have got together to pick what we consider to be the best 100 games you can play on PC. There's very little science involved, and we try not to get too hung up on what games should make the cut. From year to year, our rankings and choices vary wildly as the formation and tastes of the team changes.

However, our definitive list isn't always met with a chorus of approval and cheers of 'Hear, hear!', "'Well done!', and 'Couldn't have said it better myself!', so we also have the RPS 100: Reader Edition. This is your chance to submit your ten favourite PC games of all time. Your votes will be tallied up with all the other submissions from our other readers and we will produce a list of the community's top 100.

We've just finished revealing what we currently consider to be the Best PC games of all time and now it's your turn.

Using this very Google Form you can submit up to ten votes for your favourite PC games of all time. I will then tally them up with all the other votes from RPS's readers and produce a list of the community's top 100.

Now, a note on scoring. The game you put in 10th place will be awarded one point, 9th place will be worth two, 8th place will be worth three, and so on until you reach your top pick, which will be worth ten points. Please write the full game name (and include the year of release if there are multiple titles in a series with the same name, such as Doom (1993) and Doom (2016)). If in doubt, check how the game is titled on Steam.

Last year, I implemented a change to create a greater variety of games on the list. I combined series scores, so if one reader voted for Civilization IV and another voted for Civilization VI, the scores of both were combined and the entry would be for the Civilization series. I also shared the breakdown of the votes for each title in the entry, so you could see which was most popular within the series.

I will be doing the same again this year, as we saw a lot more games that wouldn't have made the cut otherwise. However, I will try to do a better job of separating out games that are very different from one another even if they are in the same series. Warcraft 3 and World of Warcraft are both Warcraft games, but, admittedly, they aren't similar games. I would ask for some leeway on this, though, as not every example is clear cut. Should Alpha Centauri be counted among the Civilization games? Are Final Fantasy XIV and Final Fantasy Tactics - The Ivalice Chronicles truly worlds away from the other games in the Final Fantasy series?

This does also mean that one-shot games can struggle to compete against games which are part of longrunning series. After all, Crimson Skies isn't just competing against Microsoft Flight Simulator (2020), it is competing against votes for any and all Microsoft Flight Simulator games ever released. Unfortunately, this is a cost of the system, but I prefer the variety that comes from seeing more games represented instead of several separate entries for games within the same series.

We also invite you to tell us why you've chosen each game. This is entirely voluntary, you can simply enter the game titles if you would prefer. However, I'll choose a selection of what readers have said about winning games so we can better understand why the RPS community loves these games. Try not to write any more than 100 words. If you have more to say you can always drop it in the comments of the list when we publish it at the end of the year.

To cast your votes, please make sure you complete this form by 5pm GMT on Sunday, December 6th.

#3744. GameStop CEO slams 'code-in-a-box' games in the wake of GTA 6's discless release

"The decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers."

Ryan Cohen, CEO of GameStop - the self-proclaimed "world's largest retail gaming and trade-in destination" - is not happy with the emerging trend of games releasing without discs. Per the CEO, the industry's move away from physical games and towards a digital-only future is harmful to both consumers and businesses.

In an interview with Bloomberg, Cohen explained: "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend. Unquestionably, the decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers, and it’s also hurt GameStop."

These comments come in the wake of GTA 6's launch. The game, expected to be the biggest video game launch of all time, is not shipping on discs at all. Even if you purchase a physical copy of the game, what you will actually take home is a 'code in a box' - giving you a code you can redeem on your console of choice that entitles you to a digital version of the game. GTA 6 is not the first game to do this, but it is the most high-profile. Similarly to discs, codes are also region-locked (at least on the PS5), meaning that the proliferation of codes as a format isn't even helping make games more readily available in certain markets.

Cohen notes he's been in conversation with "the obvious [publishers]" but that he's had little sway on their plans. "Of course they don’t like [trade-ins] because removing a used copy eliminates an alternative to buying new," he told Bloomberg. "They're taking away competition."

Though Cohen doesn't name GTA 6 specifically in the Bloomberg interview, it's clear that he's talking about Rockstar's megaton launch (he explicitly tweeted "GTA. On a disc. In a case. On your shelf. Like if you still want a physical copy" two days ago). The lack of trade-in potential is clearly harming his business; the Bloomberg article reveals pre-owned and refurbished products make up 22% of the GameStop's sales, down 32 percent from the same time a year ago.

Of course, the proliferation of game-in-a-box products doesn't end with GTA 6. Sony plans to stop producing physical discs for new PlayStation games starting in January 2028, moving to a digital-only model despite pushback from consumers and certain developers and publishers. The outcry is doing little to influence Sony's decision, however.

Disc or no disc, GTA 6 is expected to cross $2bn in its opening weekend, and at the moment that is looking like a conservative figure, too. It's estimated the game has sold well over 19.05m units at the time of writing. Despite the astronomical sales, though, employees at Rockstar are still worried about layoffs. Additionally, a tribunal between the studio and fired IWBG union members (who were fired for apparent breaches of their NDAs) just concluded, though the verdict may not arrive for many weeks or months.

If you need a hand with any of the myriad things GTA 6 asks you to do, you can read Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

#3743. Nvidia's latest graphics card driver appears to be unnecessarily writing to PC SSDs, something that's dumb, annoying and definitely warrants reverting

Ooh, an Nvidia-related story that isn't about their now former CEO allegedly getting amorous with someone. I wonder what it's abou-oh. Oh no. It looks like Nvidia's latest GeForce driver, 621.24, is needlessly writing vast amounts of data to PC SSDs.

As noted by PC Gamer, reports of driver 621.24 writing more than it should to SSDs have popped up across various forums and Reddit.

Some instances of the bug, which doesn't appear to be affecting everyone, have the driver writing up to 30GB every hour. For context, it'd take a bugged driver writing that much thousands of hours to break a gaming SSD with a typical endurance rating in the hundreds of terabytes. However, that doesn't mean this is anything less than a pretty bad bug. As such, reverting to the previous driver, 621.01, is a good idea if you're on 621.24 and suspect it of writing chunks of gigabytes to your SSD.

In order to check if that's going on, open task manager, head to the 'details' tab, right click on the column header, click 'select columns', select 'I/O write bytes' from the menu of check boxes that brings up, then look for 'NVDisplay.Container.exe'. The number next that exe is in bytes, so you'll need to do a bit of maths to work out if it's writing mere MB or globs of GB.

Bizarrely, the affected 621.24 driver still hasn't been pulled by Nvidia as of writing, meaning it can still be downloaded by people who might not be aware of any issues and think 'ooh, haven't checked I'm on the latest driver in a while.' The driver was released on November 12th, so it's not a brand new arrival that the company just haven't had a chance to look into yet.

Here's hoping that it is fixed or replaced ASAP, if it hasn't been by the time you read this. AMD look to have dealt with a similar issue recently, and I'd like to think driver updates across all cards aren't going to be some form of permanent Russian roulette going forwards.

Edia has announced Kendo Rage 1&2, a two-game collection featuring side-scrolling action game Kendo Rage and fighting game sequel Kendo Rage 2. It will launch for PlayStation 5, Switch, and PC via Steam on March 18, 2023.

Kendo Rage first launched for Suepr Famicom in January 1993 in Japan, followed by Super Nintendo Entertainment System in October 1993 in North America. The sequel, which never saw a localized release, launched for Super Famicom in March 1995 in Japan, followed by PlayStation in November 1995.

#3741. World of Warcraft: Forever review: The first proper MMO adventure I've been on in years

A hopeful rebirth for the old-school MMO formula.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

World of Warcraft: Forever has, much as the original World of Warcraft did back in 2004, completely consumed my life. I write about games for a living, mind, so the attention vortex it has wrought upon me is primarily professional obligation, rather than just irresponsibility.

What is it?: A reimagining of 2004's World of Warcraft, with new balancing, lighting, dungeons, and items.Expect to pay: A monthly subscription of $14.99/£10.99. Optional race and early-game zone behind a £25.99/$30 paywall.Developer: Blizzard EntertainmentPublisher: Blizzard EntertainmentReviewed on: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060, AMD Ryzen 7 5800 8-Core Processor, 16GB RAM, Force MP600 SSDMultiplayer?: YesLink: Official site

But at the time of writing, it has been 443 hours since Forever's launch. I have spent 147 of those hours asleep (less, but let's just pretend I've been getting a solid eight), leaving around 296 hours of my waking mind. 230 of them have been spent playing World of Warcraft.

That's a deeply concerning amount of time if I wasn't getting a salary to review it—it has been part of my 9-5. I've also often been keeping the game open while I, you know, feed and bathe myself and do chores. So we're probably just in the realm of 'moderately worrying' rather than 'cause for a wellness check'.

Don't worry, I intend to take a break soon: But during those 230 hours, I have hit level 60, entered 31 dungeons, completed 941 quests, levelled engineering, mining, and first aid to 300, and apparently /waved at other players 50 times. Which are rookie numbers that I need to get up.

But I've also found myself taking in the scenery, laughing at my poor luck at bottles, whining about the drop rates of basilisk brains, splitting mining nodes with party members, mercilessly grinding ogres into paste for my first mount, and talking to more strangers while questing than I have in years of playing more modern, streamlined MMOs.

I'm not pointing this out to simply cast aside the role of nostalgia in my enjoyment, but I do think nostalgia can only carry an attention span so far. It certainly doesn't keep 230 hours of medically inadvisable gameplay afloat on its own. There's something else going on here; something special that's been unearthed.

All of the things that made an old-school MMO like the original WoW so deeply enthralling back in 2004 are not simply dated, to be cast aside as an inferior form of videogame.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

The crappy drop rates, the fighting over tags, the running everywhere (there is so much running everywhere) while not always justified, is part of an experience that's stronger for its inconveniences. The friction burn you get from jutting up against a game that's occasionally just hostile to you. All of that connects you to the world, and the people in it, in a very real way.

First, I want to talk about what Forever itself has actually brought to the table. After all, much of what I've talked about already has been reverence paid to a series of design decisions that were made over 20 years ago.

In the here and now, though, Forever has around 1,000 new quests (the original WoW is estimated to've had somewhere in the mid-2,000s, so that's approximately 30-50% more Warcraft), nine new dungeons, and two new major levelling zones in Mount Hyjal and The Riverglades.

To encourage and support levelling alts, Blizzard's added a new mechanic in the Legacy tree—a genuinely cool feature that encourages you to level alts (or do endgame achievements and raids) to unlock perks, like making levelling slightly easier by giving you a small heal when you kill an enemy in the open world, or by giving you more resources when you gather things.

Then there's the retooled class and item balance, the latter of which is my one, very mild point of disappointment: There's an increasing amount of trinkets and weapons I've kept around for specific use cases, sure, but at least while levelling, the fantasy of equipping an anti-worgen sword to do some worgen-killing quests (as so often quoted in Blizzard's promotional material) hasn't quite panned out. That's not to say it's gone by the wayside completely, though.

I've seen a two-handed axe that lets you get mining nodes, a knife that lets you skin humanoids, gloves that increase your mining skill, boots that let you walk under water, and so on. It's just not a core part of the levelling experience.

It does also improve somewhat when you get into the later levels. For instance, I now have a two-handed questing sword green that I'll keep in my bags basically forever because it lets me spin around like a propeller to slow my fall speed: And I'm a Warrior, so that's a hugely useful traversal tool for someone without any way to slow fall.

Professions have also had a total facelift, and for the first time, I'm actually levelling crafting and gathering skills on my characters because of it.

Not only do crafting ones like blacksmithing actually give you really good gear as you level up (rather than just a couple of big capstone items) but all professions can now turn in writs and crates, buying new recipes via the latter and unlocking them with a rep grind via the former.

The new zones are both excellent—the Riverglades is pretty, but not out of place, whereas Hyjal is a satisfying (and very efficient) climb up a mythological mountain ruined by war, with some legitimately cool questlines to it. In both, questing is enough of a breeze that it does feel almost too easy, with Hyjal smoothing over the typically arduous 58-60 grind completely. But they're not any more efficient than, say, The Burning Crusade's better zones, which is a level of kayfabe-breaking I can get behind.

But until you hit that point, Forever's newness is downright subtle. A chain here, a few fetch quests there. Just enough to make questing in every zone worth it, just enough to even out the occasional, clunky speedbumps.

With Riverglades being level 38, and Mount Hyjal not mattering until the final stretch, Forever partially buries the lede, and you'd be forgiven for thinking it a touch unambitious. But with Blizzard's commitment to add new Riverglade-style zones and questlines to the game in the years to come, it's going to keep morphing into something new with the passing years, and what's there—when you get to it—is plainly impressive.

Such as Forever's new dungeons. I've done seven out of the new nine crawls, and while they're a little more mechanically dense than the vanilla predecessors (bosses sometimes have like, two moves) I've been fascinated by just how well that old-school design has been emulated.

With the exception of Alcaz Island, these things are sprawling, time-consuming romps. And, while controversial, the changes to dungeon XP (putting the majority of it in their quests while lowering the amount you get from mobs) has made completing them an adventure.

I recently knocked out Sunken Temple's questline, but the world-trotting, multiple quest-chain journey to get all my pre-requisites had me doing another unrelated dungeon a second time, fighting my way to the top of a troll fortress in the Hinterlands, helping out a drunk dwarf, and speaking to the spirit of a fallen Horde warrior to get his hipflask.

So when it was time to finally darken the door of the Sunken Temple and get it all done, I felt accomplished. Like I'd not just rocked up to a portal to get some fat loots, but that I'd actually—like an adventurer might—spent considerable time researching, preparing, and bracing myself for the place.

Didn't stop us forgetting that the Shade of Eranikus summons all the currently-alive dragon adds to him and getting absolutely mauled, but hey-ho.

More to the point, my XP reward for that journey felt considerably far more potent than if I'd simply hopped in there to rinse it 5 times. And I might have skipped it if the XP reward wasn't mostly dispensed via questing. I won't say dungeon XP isn't an issue for some players, but for me, the exercise works.

There hasn't just been an RTX-on style filter slapped over Azeroth, this is all bespoke."

And while you're running around the world, forced to jog ignobly between major locations, Forever's new lighting system and draw distance shines through. The reason these lighting changes aren't in retail yet is because, primarily, they're hand-crafted.

Durotar has these darling oversaturated blue shadows, Felwood bathes everything in a sickly green, Duskwood's mist hangs thick in the air, and the lightning that crackles over the Blasted Lands actually casts electric blue light across the stones of Nethergarde Keep.

But there are subtle changes, too. You can see Nordrassil, the world tree at the top of Mount Hyjal, from Durotar—as well as other zones on the continent. Dun Morogh and Winterspring have uniquely hostile snowstorm blizzards that cut out visibility entirely, similar to Tanaris' sandstorms.

There hasn't just been an RTX-on style filter slapped over Azeroth, this is all bespoke, and it's made all of my journeys that much more atmospheric. I've had to stop just to take in the godrays pushing through the canopy of Ashenvale, or the burning sunset descending on the seas of Stormwind Harbor.

More importantly, these effects really pull out the strengths of that old-school mode of design. Both the 2004 version of World of Warcraft and Forever understand that in order for a world to feel massive, it needs to be difficult to traverse sometimes. In order for it to be social, there needs to be a level of unfairness that being social will overcome.

I thoroughly enjoyed World of Warcraft: Midnight, the latest expansion in modern World of Warcraft, when I reviewed it for launch. I thought the questlines, which I can remember the glossy cinematics and major storybeats of, were engaging enough. And I still think its new revamped Silvermoon is gorgeous, and a complete flex from the studio's art team.

I could not, however, tell you a single thing about my questing experience that wasn't dictated to me by the game. Yes, I liked certain story beats or character conversations, but the actual experience of hitting stuff? It's a blur. I flew somewhere, I pushed my buttons, I interacted with something. I flew somewhere else, and you know what I did there? I pushed more buttons.

In contrast, I've been playing Forever for almost three weeks, and I've already made memories. On a jog to an annoying Scarlet Monastery dungeon questline that sent me to Desolace, I met up with two dwarven brothers (or husbands? They had the same second name) who were making the journey. We joined up with more people to kill a bunch of high-level skeletons, and barely got through an overpull by the skin of our teeth.

In Stranglethorn Vale, a kindly shadow priest six levels higher than me partied up to kill some pirates, then pointed out that there was a good questline that could be done by scavenging beach bottles. They got theirs on their first try. I, for some reason, had to pick up 26 of the damn things.

On another journey, I decided to try and grab my fire-hardened mail armor for a warrior questline, which sent my alliance character all the way into The Barrens, to Razorfen Kraul. This is not a great dungeon to do if you're an alliance character, so the pickings were slim. Which meant that I not only tanked the whole thing as Fury, but that the folks I was with were chill enough to do a quick road-trip to Feralas with me to get another dungeon quest.

The point being, I only had these memorable experiences and spoke to these people because I was being, and I know this is a bad word for a lot of MMO players, inefficient. Absolute bastard questlines made me do something far out of the way. And every single time I've played along, I wound up having a lovely time meeting similarly stubborn folks and making new friends.

A lot of these inconveniences, carried over from vanilla and left alone in Forever, are there to push you and people you meet organically, out in the world, into close quarters and camaraderie. To do "kill X" quests, you need to intentionally party up with that random night elf warrior, rather than just pass them by. To get certain questlines accomplished at the level they're given, you need to ask for help in general chat.

Some chains will send you to some random city, forcing you to learn the most efficient boat route to get there—or to simply leave that quest in your log until you next happen to pop your head into Darnassus. The travel time makes the world feel big. The encouraged cooperation makes it feel alive and social. And all that friction produces friendships—these quests suck to do on your own but are so often a breeze to do together. Or, at the very least, they're more entertaining with company.

This is why it doesn't just feel like nostalgia to me. It's the rub of the whole thing. I am not enjoying these quests because, at some time in the past, I had a nice innocent memory surrounding them that I'm reliving. It's actually all about what's happening in the present: Grouping up with people, striking up conversations, sharing in misery as it takes a full 45 minutes to fill our bags with pirate hats.

I'm honestly just marvelling about the fact that, in 2026, that this sort of design still works. It works tremendously well. Blizzard's new campfire mechanic, which I like a lot, is just a cherry-on-top-nudge towards striking up the conversations I was already having anyway.

So many times, my purposefully chill vibes have been met with genuine kindness: People stay on to help you finish quests they've already completed, they show you new questlines. Sometimes it's a tit-for-tat. A shaman helped me out with my level 50 warrior quest in exchange for me helping him kill an elite somewhere, which hey, fair dos.

This all culminated in an incident where I joined in for a random kill quest in my mid-40s. A priest, around their mid-40s as well, commented that man, a lotta folks had their mounts already! Myself included. I'd spent a few hours mining over 200 Iron Ores and killing cave ogres, like a maniac.

I asked how far off they were. They said they had 80 gold out of 90. I threw 15 gold at them before I realised what I was doing.

This isn't to humblebrag, mind. My grinding had produced a surplus of cash that I wasn't really spending: But it was like I'd been suddenly possessed by the spirit of Christmases past, future, and present. I gave a complete stranger a significant amount of money with the complete understanding I'd never talk to them again. Because I felt like being nice, because so many people had been nice to me.

I do understand the yearning for flight paths, for lower respec costs, for shared mob tagging, and for quests that don't require your character to walk the circumference of the earth. And if none of that's to your taste, then hey, fine—but more than anything, Forever's proven to me that those flying mount doomers back in The Burning Crusade might've been onto something.

I still enjoy 'theme park' MMOs, but Forever is such a deeply exciting prospect to me. It's a second chance for this older, slower, more social form of videogame to have a renaissance. Before booting up Forever on November 4, I couldn't tell you the last time I had an adventure (an organic one, not one delivered to me through a storyline) in an MMORPG. Two weeks later, and I've had several, and I keep logging on and embarking on these long, arduous quest chains because I'm excited to have more.

Forever is such rare air. A major MMO studio has been given the blessing to revamp a 20+ year old version of a game and add to it. And while it's already added a considerable amount, Forever feels like proof that, given enough exposure in the spotlight, people could actually like a new MMO with its design sensibilities.

And as a fan of lots of different kinds of MMOs—be they slow-paced adventures like Forever or on-rails dungeon-rinsing theme parks like Final Fantasy 14—I want this genre to have the kind of actual diversity it deserves. More MMOs than World of Warcraft should get to take this sort of risk. More MMOs should be able to take it slow.

Until that new game comes, however, I'll happily play Forever, and I cannot wait to roll up an alt to start doing it all over again.

A hopeful rebirth for the old-school MMO formula.

Harvey's history with games started when he first begged his parents for a World of Warcraft subscription aged 12, though he's since been cursed with Final Fantasy 14-brain and a huge crush on G'raha Tia. He made his start as a freelancer, writing for websites like Techradar, The Escapist, Dicebreaker, The Gamer, Into the Spine—and of course, PC Gamer. He'll sink his teeth into anything that looks interesting, though he has a soft spot for RPGs, soulslikes, roguelikes, deckbuilders, MMOs, and weird indie titles. He also plays a shelf load of TTRPGs in his offline time. Don't ask him what his favourite system is, he has too many.

#3740. GTA 6 has replaced websites with social media and phone apps because "it didn't feel necessary"

The internet of today is a far cry from the days when Grand Theft Auto 5 was released, which is partly why Rockstar didn't bring back its own satirical version of the web in GTA 6.

The web pages of Lifeinvadder, Bleeter, and Eyefind have instead given way to BuckMe, Scooter Bros, and WhatUp apps. The reason? Smartphone apps just made more sense.

"It didn't feel necessary for us," Rockstar North boss Rob Nelson told Kotaku. "We definitely wanted to lean into apps and create these apps."

Though some of the apps in GTA 6 perform similar tasks to the web of old, Nelson said the team didn't want players to be distracted from the game's detailed open world by staring at screens. That also extends to getting players to appreciate the value of money, and witnessing the progression of Jason and Lucia as they go from pawnshop robberies to staging major bank heists.

"They don't really need websites to be buying a lot of shit, you know what I mean, and so everything grows very organically," Nelson said, adding that websites may return in the future.

"I remember asking Stu Petri, our head of 2D and UI, about websites, and he was like, 'For what? What do you need it for?' So, that was it," he added.

In materials supplied by Rockstar ahead of our review, Sam Grosset (associate UI director at the studio) also explained that a lot of thought went into how the apps work, and how easily the phone needed to fit into your play style in order for it to work as effectively as possible.

"We ensure the UI feels like a natural extension of the game world, supporting players without interrupting gameplay or breaking immersion, unless necessary to do so," said Grosset. "The UI should be complementary to the game and appropriate for each scenario. It was a big shift for our phone interface to be in-hand, but it supports that feeling of playing as Jason or Lucia and helps us stay embedded in the world."

Rockstar would continually "raise the bar, question assumptions, explore new possibilities, and learn through rigorous testing and iteration" in order to make these apps - and the UX/UI in general - feel in line with the production quality of the rest of the game.

In Eurogamer's GTA 6 review, Chris Tapsell awarded the open-world crime game five stars, raving about its absurd level of detail, compelling characters, exciting action and of its big heart.

If you're looking to spend the next several days playing Rockstar's latest hit, Eurogamer's GTA 6 walkthrough has detailed guides on everything from individual missions, to core mechanics like the new Wanted Level, and relationship and romance.

The release of GTA 6 has been a swirling vortex which most companies have actively worked to avoid. Beyond avoiding this period for launching anything, lots of other studios have opted to avoid putting out any substantial updates on their games either. Now that the initial fervor is dying down a little, the team behind Palworld is putting feelers out on letting fans know what's coming on that front.

Over on Twitter, John 'Bucky' Buckley, the head of communications and publishing at Pocketpair, tweeted about whether the coast was clear. "Is it OK to start talking about Palworld 1.1 and Palfarm now?" he posted, hinting at the Grand Theft Auto 6-sized blanket that now lays over the collective medium.

Last week, he was quite clear that we wouldn't be hearing about the next major update for Palworld, or any of the game's spin-offs, for a minute because it just wasn't the right time. Rockstar's gargantuan sandbox was sucking all the air out of the room.

Is it OK to start talking about Palworld v1.1 and Palfarm now? 😇November 24, 2026

Not everyone was playing GTA 6 at launch, nor does every person into video games care for it, but enough do that it's important to be wary of the news cycle and the attention it's getting at the moment. Headline space is predominantly going toward Leonida for the time being, and I say that as someone who's writing about it in some form on the daily.

That'll loosen up as the weeks go on, because there'll be less to cover regarding Jason and Lucia, and people's attention will start to scatter again. Those Palworld players who've departed for sunnier skies will come back, ready to see what's going on in the realm of monster collecting.

I'm not sure that's right now, but it'll be soon. The first week or two is really the peak, and then other games can start poking back into the limelight. World of Warcraft: Forever and Final Fantasy 14 are happening, as well. The industry is still turning.

Once the Palfarm and Palworld 1.1 updates arrive, we'll make sure you know. It's just extra helpful if there's less chance they get immediately buried under yet more Leonida-shaped shenanigans.

#3737. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 was October's biggest game in the US, but it wasn't enough to crack 2026's best-selling top 10

Despite its somewhat muted critical reception, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 has predictably topped the US video game charts in October. The Infinity Ward-developed shooter was October's best-selling game in the US across digital and retail, beating the month's other big-hitters, including Gears of War: E-Day and Star Wars: Galactic Racer.

That's according to market analysis firm Circana's latest US market report, which revealed Modern Warfare 4 was October's leader in dollar sales. This marks the 19th-year running that a Call of Duty game topped the charts in its release month, a streak that began with November 2008's COD: World at War.

However, despite a successful October, Modern Warfare 4 hasn't managed to land in Circana's top ten list of year-to-date biggest sellers. In fact, the only COD title on the list is the Black Ops 2 port released this summer. NBA 2K27 continues to lead Circana's ranking, having overtaken Resident Evil: Requiem last month to secure the top spot. It's a reverse of Circana's September report, when NBA 2K27 failed to lead its own debut month but claimed the top spot in the year-to-date list. Here's the list of the top 10 year-to-date:

Away from Modern Warfare 4, October saw the release of several other well-performing and critically acclaimed games, and six of the top ten were new releases. That hasn't stopped Circana from posting 14 percent lower spending on games compared to October last year. Analyst Mat Piscatella noted much of that dip can be attributed to a big slump in mobile spending, and also because October 2025 was particularly strong, with both Battlefield 6 and Pokémon Legends: Z-A releasing. Here's October's top 10:

In Eurogamer's Modern Warfare 4 review, Dom Peppiatt awarded it four stars, writing: "Modern Warfare 4 represents the highest tide for Call of Duty in seven years. Infinity Ward needed to pull off a balancing act I don't envy; injecting just enough nostalgia into a series propped up with so many conventions and expectations there's barely room for anything new, alongside enough innovation and intrigue to keep people interested."

#3736. Darkest Dungeon 2's next bit of DLC is a short run, combat focused gauntlet where you must do everything in your power to please the audience

The original Darkest Dungeon may have gotten some new DLC earlier this year, but that doesn't mean that Red Hook Studios are abandoning their sequel. No, in fact the next bit of DLC for Darkest Dungeon 2 was teased only a couple of weeks ago, with a new trailer shared today actually showing off what it's all about.

It's called The Butcher's Asylum, as pleasant a name as any other, and it's a "stand alone gladiatorial arena game mode," that's due for release sometime in 2027. "The long-silent bells of the remote Asylum ring once more - souring the valley below with discordant and unsettling vibrations," the DLC's Steam page describes. "Garish heraldry, hastily stitched by unskilled hands, festoons the hilltop. Deep within the crumbling masonry of the Asylum, frenzied inmates compete in merciless bloodsport with monsters corralled the kingdom over. And to the victors of these debauched contests, the Butcher’s favour: a cure for their madness."

This DLC isn't veering too far away from its roguelite origins, as it is still run-based, just on the shorter side and focusing more on the combat system. On your runs you'll need to prepare for the fights ahead, come across "insane enemy combinations never before possible," and spin a fun wheel which nets you prizes like new battle modifiers, charms and jinxes. There's also a new crowd meter, "a unique feature to the Asylum, can grant powerful effects to your team if you cater to the Crowd's demands. Failing to do so will only earn their scorn which raises the stakes and puts your success in jeopardy!"

The Butcher's Asylum also introduces a new playable character, The Ringmaster. You pick her up by winning bouts in the arena, and then you can recruit her in any game mode. She also serves as the narrator for the DLC, likely because of the passing of the main game's narrator Wayne June; Red Hook made clear earlier this year that they would never use generative AI to recreate June's voice, so I'm glad to see they haven't backstracked here.

Leonida deserves to be explored with friends.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I honestly can't recall the last time I took such delight in existing within a virtual world as the way I have with Grand Theft Auto 6's Leonida. Rockstar has delivered on its promise of both breadth and depth—the map is huge, but utterly stuffed with detail. Large, open highways shrink into single lanes surrounded by construction that force me to slam the brakes. Sidewalks sparse with pedestrians eventually lead to densely packed retail areas, restaurants, and clubs.

Pockets of culture erupt all over: the sheer redneckery of Port Gellhorn, the Latin culture that permeates Little Cuba, and the affluent snootiness of Capri that has cops flinging microaggressions in every direction. You don't need to undertake any missions in these areas to understand the people that live here—Rockstar has nailed so much of the environmental storytelling and the conversations between NPCs you'll stumble on as you roam.

It's a world that, when I first ventured into it, I had no interest in exploring in a multiplayer setting. I spent an ungodly amount of time in GTA 5's Online mode when it first released. I was there on the ground for its incredibly shaky launch (I made a character and then got stuck in that birdseye view loading screen for hours, incredible stuff) and continued to sink time into it over the years, particularly during Covid.

And I like it well enough, but its novelty has waned over the last decade. Its core experience is inherently different from what singleplayer brings, and I had yearned to return to a world less about blowing other players up with flying motorbikes and more about, well, blowing non-players up with regular motorbikes.

But after 60 hours roaming around Leonida and witnessing what it has to offer? I now want nothing more than for Rockstar to spin this map into the next generation of Online. Even outside of missions and driving around, there are so many little things that I would kill to do with pals.

Grab a pack of brewskis from the convenience store, hop in a boat, and go fishing. Throw on our best all-American attire and get down and dirty in some mud racing. Seek out other players meticulously planning a jewellery store hold-up, only to swoop in and steal the goods for ourselves. Hit up the gym for a little workout before nipping to a nearby restaurant for a bite to eat. Leonida is a place that is so rife with things to do, and I can imagine doing almost all of them with some buddies by my side.

It's also the perfect opportunity for Rockstar to introduce things that are sorely missing for me right now. A lack of safehouses makes sense with GTA 6's offline story, but I yearn to buy highrise apartments and suburban houses. Maybe even buy a business or two, for a little side cash. There's also the matter of that gigantic casino and the go-kart track that are currently inaccessible but the latter of which is donning a large "COMING SOON" sign. It feels like I'm being taunted. Surely you wouldn't put these things in the game with no intention of opening them at some point… right?

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

And even as someone who was never interested in nor dabbled with GTA Online's flourishing roleplaying scene, I've encountered so many instances where I've thought roleplaying in Leonida actually be pretty darn neat. I could become a RydeMe driver, or a Snapmatic influencer, or a backwater recluse who lives off the land. And when the game comes to PC? The potential for bending the world to account for even more professions becomes all the greater.

Rockstar hasn't actually said a damn thing about GTA 6 Online right now, but it feels inevitable. Leonida is the biggest playground the developer has given players to date, and unleashing players across its sprawling map is Online's natural evolution. And, y'know, considering how much money GTAO has made over the last 13 years, I'm almost certain that Rockstar won't leave that kind of opportunity on the table.

Mollie spent her early childhood deeply invested in games like Killer Instinct, Toontown and Audition Online, which continue to form the pillars of her personality today. She can often be found causing mischief in Final Fantasy 14, using those experiences to write neat things about her favourite MMO. When she's not staring at her bunny girl she can be found sweating out rhythm games, pretending to be good at fighting games or spending far too much money at her local arcade.

#3733. As Rockstar's alleged "union busting" tribunal hearing comes to a close amid GTA 6 launch, judge pledges to deliver verdict "as quickly as I possibly can"

Closing statements in Rockstar and IWGB's employment tribunal case - revolving around the GTA 6 developer's alleged 'union busting' and the firing of 34 employees - have now been read, bringing the hearing to an end. There's currently no timeline for a verdict, however, with one commentator suggesting a judgement could take weeks or months to arrive.

The case, which began in September and has included evidence from 23 claimants in the months since, must now be considered by the judge, who will determine if Rockstar unfairly dismissed employees in breach of their employment rights. Rockstar has been accused of unlawfully firing workers for being part of a union, but the GTA developer insists employees were dismissed for breaching confidentiality agreements.

People Makes Games' Chris Bratt has been following the case closely and reporting on proceedings as they've unfolded. With closing statements now complete, Bratt quoted Judge Lucy Wiseman as saying, "I cannot give a time frame for producing the judgement in this case. What I will say is that I will use my best endeavors to get that judgement out as quickly as I possibly can."

However, Bratt suggests it could be ""anywhere from a few weeks up to a few months before we actually hear the judgement", noting "The firings themselves, let's not forget, happened over a year ago now. This has been a slog."

One fired Rockstar worker involved in the case spoke with Bratt after the closing statements to share their thoughts. "Honestly it's just sort of blended together," they said. "It’s been so long, that after the first six months or so it became the new depressing reality. I'm hoping the judgement will release us from it."

Last month, the conclusion of the tribunal hearing was delayed after cross examination of witnesses ran long.

Yesterday's closing statements come at a time when all eyes are on GTA 6 as it finally releases this week, concluding years of development for both current and former employees. Many of those workers involved in the case urged players to support the game despite the legal dispute.

Additionally, Rockstar employees are currently voting on whether they want recognised union representation at the studio. If the vote passes, it would be the largest recognised union across the entirety of the UK video game industry. The deadline for union votes is 26th November.

Break into Boogie’s laptop using clues found in the apartment

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The GTA 6 laptop password appears in Chapter 3, when Jason and Lucia end up borrowing an apartment from a friend of a friend called Boogie. In the bedroom, there’s a conspicuous open laptop that requires a password to get into. If you’re curious, all the clues can be found in the apartment, and you’ll get a pretty nice ride out of it, too – at least once you find the location it hints towards.

The GTA 6 laptop pass word is Muffins Queen 15, found from various clues around the house. Below I'll run through all the info you need to find what you want.

When you first find the laptop you’ll be able to put in a few guesses, but none of them will be right. Instead, you’ll need to unlock the correct prompts by searching around your safehouse. First, head to the entrance hallway to find the shrine to Boogie’s dog (above).

By examining the picture you’ll find out the dog’s name was Muffins. But the password is a bit more secure than that. Head back into the bedroom to find the next clue on the bedside table.

The notebook shows Muffins wearing a crown, but that’s not all. Flip it over to find a message: “Class of ‘15 reunion next Friday.”

Once you’ve done that, you have all the clues you need. Go back to the laptop and follow the prompts to enter “Muffins,” “Queen,” and “15.” Once inside, don’t forget to flip through Boogie’s messages to find a clue about where to find your reward: Vanessa's Pink Porsche, in the garage near a restaurant near Auntie’s Place. You’ll automatically pick up the code to get in, too.But you might not be able to find the garage immediately – it’s not marked on the map. #3731. "Everyone agrees it's more fun this way": Toby Fox won't tell his team how Deltarune ends until they've built enough of it

"Just when the story reached a critical moment, I stopped reading…"

Toby Fox is a purposefully mysterious person. It was probably a wise choice on his part, obfuscating his current appearance with everyone's favourite annoying dog, essentially never speaking aloud in livestreams and instead using a text-to-speech bot, and posting only when there's notable enough Deltarune updates of if it would be very funny. But as it turns out, that sense of mystery extends to the team that's making Deltarune too, as Fox won't tell his devs how the game ends until they've built enough of it.

Earlier this week, the fall edition of the Deltarune newsletter went out, offering a brief update on the game's next and sixth chapter. That one's apparently now a "structurally complete draft that can be played from the beginning to the end," but that doesn't mean it's quite ready for release, as "some important scenes and details are still undercooked in their presentation." I'd expect a 2027 release for this chapter, which is going to be a shorter one too.

But in typical tricky Tony fashion, there's an update for chapter seven where he makes it sound like no one but him knows how the whole game is going to end. "Well, we've only just started…," he explains of the progress. "I read out the events and dialogue of Chapter 7 to the team. However, just when the story reached a critical moment, I stopped reading… I told my team they need to complete more of the game before I tell them what happens. Everyone agrees it's more fun this way."

I'm glad they all think it's fun, the wait for me personally certainly ain't. I do wonder if this speaks to a certain anxiety over how the game will shape up. Following the release of chapter five I was subjected to all manner of theories about what's to come by my partner gorging on YouTube videos from folks who mostly just seem quite excited about it all, even if a lot of them sound wrong. So I imagine there must be a little bit of weight to all of those varying expectations.

Fox did note in the newsletter that "unlike every other Chapter, I actually feel like I know what I'm doing this time, so I have a lot of confidence...!" so perhaps I'm speaking a load of hogwash! That said, I'm furious that a character called Apple Girlington didn't make it into chapter five, so you can expect to hear from my lawyers, Mr. Fox.

The world wants me to write more about Grand Theft Auto 6 and I bravely answer "No". Last week, I obtained 50% of the endings available in Queen's Domain, the best videogame to release in the year 2026. The next 50% require, well, a lot of nook-scouring and cranny-uncovering—many more hours of gameplay which I am preserving for myself as a Christmas holiday treat.

And when I do, I suspect I might make a little (just a little) use of this rad Queen's Domain map by a creator called Leny15. Barely a week ago I wrote that "I suspect a cross-section of [Queen's Domain's] goliath, entwined map would make for a killer bit of wall art". Well, I was right. Here it is and it looks rad as hell.

No, really. Even if you're not a Queen's Domain player—or maybe especially if you're not—take a look at this thing. It's one thing to wander these maps as a player, it's another to get a totally flexible birdseye view of how dense, twisty and interconnected they are. I will never stop being blown away by how knotty and elaborate this game is; I love it.

I will also never believe I have actually explored all of it. I'll be honest, gang, I really feel like I've plumbed the depths of this game, but this map has entries for areas I ain't even heard of, and even those areas that I have heard of seem to contain secret sub-areas I've barely touched.

My favourite feature of this thing has got to be the ability to upload your save to it, at which point it will give you a completion percentage and tick off the collectibles and secrets you've already attained (reminder that you can download your Steam cloud saves right in your browser). I was heartened to read that I have, it seems, done in about 70% of this game already. I was even more heartened to learn that the remaining 30% seems even stranger, more complicated, and more baffling than all the rest. I can't wait to check it out.

#3728. Eldritch Empathy is a Papers Please-esque roguelite about diagnosing cosmic horror creatures and trying not to lose your marbles as you do

Oh I do love an eldritch horror creature, I do, especially one that at first glance may only be slightly different from what I'm used to seeing. Eldritch Empathy, then, seems like a grand ole game to satisfy my wanton need to experience such things. It's a puzzle roguelite that isn't exactly a Papers Please-like but certainly feels reminiscent of one, where you have to "analyse corrupted creatures, purify their emotions and learn how to communicate with an eldritch being."

You kick things off by embodying Eike, a "young woman who has strange dreams and sightings of twisted creatures in the woodlands neighbouring the sleepy Swiss village she lives in." She decides to investigate these mysterious circumstances herself, where she comes upon these corrupted critters in the woods. You need to thoroughly inspect them, using a book to determine what is going on with them and what they need exactly; it's akin to checking the passport rulebook in Papers Please, hence the comparison.

After figuring out what's going on with these creatures, you then "use and transform symbols to create paths through the creatures' insides. You may use care and precision to navigate to the correct corrupted emotion you have identified from your investigation and purify it. You may also use your tools to cause harm. Whatever you choose, your actions will have consequences." Ominous! You can also plan your runs ahead of time, heading down paths that may offer you some boons here and there, like the option to restore a bit of sanity (it's one of those Lovecraftian kind of horror games, as loathe as I am that we still have to reference that guy).

Also be wary of the fact that actions you take out in the woods can affect your home and community. It's a roguelite with consequences! Mwahahha! Looks pretty neat overall, and has some tasty pixel art attached to it too. No release date just yet, but I'd assume it'll arrive no earlier than next year. You can wishlist it right here.

#3727. Warren Spector lambasts GTA 6's "billion dollar" development - 'I just hope it's is the last of its kind even if it's the best we have to offer'

"A billion dollars pays for a lot of games and a lot of salaries."

As GTA 6 finally arrives, increasingly outspoken games industry legend Warren Spector - known for seminal immersive sims including Deus Ex - has offered both praise for the game's achievements and lambasted its "billion dollar" development model, writing, "I just hope GTA 6 is the last of its kind even if it’s the best we have to offer".

Spector announced his retirement from games development in August following struggles at his OtherSide Entertainment studio, and has been vocal about the state of the games industry in the months since, notably saying anyone at EA responsible for the "travesty" of BioWare's closure should be "ashamed". And now Spector has taken on GTA 6.

"First, congratulations to everyone who worked on GTA 6. It looks like it will be a high point of sorts for our medium and our business," he wrote in a post on LinkedIn. "However… its billion dollar development cost and an undoubtedly crazy marketing budget don't represent a business model anyone else can or probably should emulate.

"That's especially true," Spector continued, "when thousands of developers are out of work. A billion dollars pays for a lot of games and a lot of salaries. Personally I'd rather have hundreds of games and full employment than one game no matter how amazing it is."

The "sure success" of GTA 6 proves a point he's made "for years", he said: "That no game that matters ships on time and/or on budget". Highlighting GTA 6's year-long delay and reported billion dollar budget, Spector suggested, "Give a game the time and money to prove its potential (key word, potential) and you have a chance of making something great. Underfund a game or force it out the door before it's ready [is] guaranteed failure no matter how much potential it has.

"So, again, congratulations," Spector concluded. "Ambition and innovation are necessary for the medium to reach its potential. I just hope GTA 6 is the last of its kind even if it's the best we have to offer."

Despite Spector's concerns, GTA 6's arrival is, as expected, already causing shockwaves across the industry. It has broken pre-order records for Xbox and PlayStation stores, smashed the all-time livestream viewer record, and apparently briefly broke Reddit too. And is its success deserved? Eurogamer's Chris Tapsell thinks so, saying it "pushes back the horizon of video games once again" in his five star GTA 6 review.

I just hope Ubisoft knows what that means from a budget perspective

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Christoph Hartmann, general manager of Massive Entertainment, says he wants the Ubisoft division to position itself as the "A24 of gaming."

Earlier this year, the Star Wars Outlaws and The Division developer's role grew substantially as the existing studio became the lead of one of the five creative houses that Ubisoft divided its studios between following its "major reset." Creative House 2 is Massive Entertainment, which was described as the home of "competitive and cooperative shooter" experiences, including The Division, Ghost Recon, and Splinter Cell.

Speaking to Variety, Hartmann explains, "I want us to be definitely not just a shooter house," citing MOBA title March of Giants as an example. He adds, "I want us to be a label which really looks after the core gamer."

He explains that the studio is "not going to do" racing, sports, or "casual kids" titles, "But could we do an RPG one day? Could we do MMO? Could I maybe do even a strategy game? Sure." He continues, "If we have the talent internally or something happens, then we bring it on."

Hartmann says his "dream" is to become "the A24 of video gaming." He explains this as "a place I describe with winning Oscars and still being commercially successful, definitely having [an] impact on what they're doing," and calling it the "coolest place" in the entertainment industry.

Ultimately, the key thing with A24 is that the distributor's films weren't overnight hits and it took a while for it to become as beloved as it is. With something like Skull and Bones or Beyond Good and Evil 2, it's hard to imagine those games not having a staggering amount of money spent on them based on their development hell.

The real challenge will be for Ubisoft to not lay off developers at the whiff of failure – or even success, as Ubisoft laid off 166 devs at Assassin's Creed and Far Cry studios last week and on the same day called Black Flag Resynced "among the industry's most successful action-adventure remakes."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

A24's biggest hit is Backrooms which made just over $400 million earlier this year, but that was the studio's first film to cross $200 million worldwide, and it took until Everything Everywhere All at Once in 2022 – a decade after it was founded – for a film to break $100 million. And even now there's only been seven movies total by A24 to reach that milestone.

So if Massive Entertainment wants to be the A24 of games, it and Ubisoft need to be realistic about what that means. The old adage of "I want shorter games with worse graphics and I'm not kidding" comes to mind.

Down 1,100 staff in 6 months, Ubisoft dumps its money into gen AI with a whole subsidiary called Motherbrain "focused on AI for gameplay."

#3725. Does GTA 6 have an 'easy mode'? Not officially, but there are two very important settings you can change to make the game less difficult

By now, you've probably heard that you cannot use cheats in GTA 6 until you complete the main story. Not only that, but enabling cheat codes also locks story progression and deactivates the ability to save. Basically, you can use cheats to have a quick crime spree and blow off some steam, then it's back to normalcy. Understandably, some gamers are a little put out with this change.

But, for anyone looking to have a slightly easier time with GTA 6 than the dev's intended experience, I come with good news: you can make the game a little bit easier by toggling two options in the game's Settings menu. If you open Settings, and then navigate to Gameplay, you'll find 'Accessible Combat' and 'Reduced Vehicle Damage' toggles. You can activate both to make GTA 6's more difficult elements a little bit easier to work through.

'Accessible Combat' decreases enemy health and makes them deal less damage to your character — the kind of rebalancing that you'd expect from a traditional difficulty slider. 'Reduced Vehicle Damage', as you'd expect, lowers the damage taken by your vehicle and allows your ride to endure more punishment. This applies to gunfire, environmental threats, and impact damage.

Toggle these settings comes with a warning from Rockstar, though. A prompt notes that enabling these modifiers will "significantly change the balance and experience of the gameplay". I've been playing around with these settings and whilst they are not a foolproof 'God Mode' by any means, you can absolutely see a difference in the game when they're enabled: Jason and Lucia take a lot more punishment from melee damage and gunshots, and I had to really try to get Jason's old banged up pickup into even the 'slightly smoking' bracket of disrepair. Your mileage may vary, but these settings, from what I can tell so far, certainly do make the game easier.

Given that cheats disable trophies and progression, these settings might be something to keep in mind if you're trying to find a smoother path through the main story of GTA 6. It's a credit to Rockstar's accessibility teams that these have been included at all - alongside the 23 other gameplay accessibility options, the 12 display options, the 70 UI options, the 24 camera options, and the 14 audio options.

"We create inclusive, intuitive, and immersive experiences for every player," noted Rockstar's associate UI director, Sam Grosset, in materials provided to Eurogamer ahead of the game's launch. "Accessibility is considered from the outset, and designing for diverse needs enables us to create better games for everyone. We wanted every player in GTA 6 to have options to play the game how they like. Whether it's selecting a larger font size, opting for a more minimal screen experience, or making a controls tweak to sprinting... the choices are open to all."

We also learned yesterday that Rockstar has made GTA 6 missions "harder to fail" by making them more open-ended, and giving players more ways to figure out how to do things in their own way.

If you need a hand with any of the myriad things GTA 6 asks you to do, you can read Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

The notorious GTA 6 leaker called it "an early Christmas gift."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Grand Theft Auto 6 leaker Cyberleek appears to have followed through on their threat to release the executable of the Xbox build of GTA 6 they put into the wild last week, calling it "an early Christmas gift" for followers and explicitly linking the leak to efforts to recreate the game on PC: "The torch passes to the open source recomp and emulation projects."

Cyberleek released a near-complete build of GTA 6 late last week, holding back only the main exe—the part that makes everything else run, basically—until either their crypto coin achieved a $15 million market cap, or November 23, whichever came first. The crypto missed badly, but time marches on, and so here we are.

The release of the exe, naturally, includes a call for more "donations" in its readme file (via Reddit) which Cyberleek said will go toward a secretive project "for the gamers." They also taunted Take-Two Interactive's efforts to track them down: "Months of takedowns, subpoenas and wallet tracing later, the hunt is still on and the uploads keep arriving. No budget makes a lock unbreakable, and no court order deletes what the internet already has."

Leaks in the game industry aren't anything new, but this case is unique: GTA 6, effectively the biggest videogame of all time, still hasn't been announced for PC, as is Take-Two's way. But the advent of AI means the game could be emulated on our platform far more quickly than was possible in the past—some modders estimated it could happen within a week.

One of the leads on the Leonida recomp project predicted that things will start to move quickly from here:

At the same time, Shayder tempered expectations in a message on the Leonida Discord, saying "it will take at least a week" for the project to reach the point where GTA will be playable on PC.

How that unofficial emulated made-with-AI build would compare to the real deal is an open question, and I strongly suspect the answer will be "not well," but even just having something GTA 6-ish playable on PC is a headache that I'm pretty sure Take-Two would rather not have to deal with. I also wonder whether it will prompt Take-Two to release GTA 6 on PC more quickly than it has with previous releases. A rumor to that effect surfaced in October and I had serious doubts, but it's possible that ongoing emulation efforts will expedite its arrival..

#3722. Public-access television is born anew in NIGHT EYE TV, a digital goggle box filled with art game curios

I am both a bit too young and a bit too very not American to have ever experienced public-access television, but it's something that's always fascinated me. For those too young to have even heard of it, or just not in the know, it essentially allowed anyone to broadcast their own shows through cable TV. A proto YouTube, if you will. It's obviously not what it was any more, given the advent of the internet, but in NIGHTEYE.TV, it may be making a digital, more interactive return.

NIGHTEYE.TV is a strange little place. I call it a place, it's a fake TV floating in a Unity default texture void, lending it a Backroomsian vibe, but even if there's not much there to ground yourself in, the goggle box is enticing all the same. It beckons you to turn it on, a series of buttons all linking to different "channels." What awaits you isn't television, however. Instead you'll find games, mostly of the weirdo, freako, sicko variety, quickly setting the tone.

🌕NIGHT EYE TV’s initial form is live!🌑 Check out the site and follow our Indiegogo campaign at www.nighteye.tv![image or embed]

In its current incarnation, it's mostly just a collection of clips of these various art games, with direct links to them hidden away in a menu, but a good collection it is. You'll find Nathalie Lawhead's Everything is Going to Be OK, Jeremy Couillard's more recent Soul Injector Commando, and Taylor McCue's He Fucked The Girl Out Of Me. Some clips are longer than others, acting as sort of segments of playthroughs, but it all feels like an exciting evolution of what public-access television was.

The ultimate goal is for it to be a curated platform where you can buy a rotating selection of games. Most of the sale goes back to the original artist, and 15% gets put into a community pool to be split amongst all of the contributors, with the last 15% going towards keeping everything running. As it stands, that's not quite ready yet. You can help make it happen, though, as right now an Indiegogo campaign is running to help it all get fully operational. Worth chucking a few quid I reckon!

You'll need to find Auntie's Place in GTA 6 once you've get the laptop password to unlock Boogie’s laptop in the Chapter 3 safehouse. The messages that gets you says there’s a surprise at Auntie’s Place, but there’s no hints as to where that is, and it’s not marked on the map as it’s not a place you can actually interact with.

To find Auntie’s Place in GTA 6, first head to Twa Ponya Tattoo parlour in the north of Vice City. Then, look across the street and you’ll see a small restaurant with a red sign. This is Auntie’s Place. It’s also around the back of Aline’s Thrift Store, if that helps.

The car isn’t at the restaurant itself. Instead, behind and to the right of it there’s a locked garage. It may have a red car parked outside. You’ll automatically have the code you need to enter if you’ve unlocked Boogie’s laptop and read his messages. If not, you’ll need to head back to the apartment and take a look around for the clues hidden there. If you get stuck, we’ve also explained where you can find them and what words they hint towards.

Inside the garage you’ll find Vanessa's Growler, a pink Pfister (Porsche) sports car. The car will automatically be added to your owned vehicles. You’ll also unlock this garage as a place to store one vehicle. It’s called the Del Rio Boulevard Garage.

#3718. Over 2 million Xbox players in the UK and US reportedly used the 'New Zealand trick' to play GTA 6 early - that's more than a third of the country's population

We already knew there'd be a frantic clamour for GTA 6 this week, and we also knew plenty of players would be eyeing up Xbox's 'New Zealand trick' to get in on the action early. But it's now being reported that a whopping 2m UK and US players took advantage of the trick - which, for context, equals more than a third of New Zealand's actual population.

Here's a quick bit of background: Rockstar's regional release schedule meant GTA 6 launched at midnight on 19th November everywhere, local time. As such, New Zealand was the first country in the world to see the hugely anticipated game go live, thanks to timezones. And because Xbox players can make purchases on any regional store easily, simply by changing their console's country, understandably impatient sorts opted to become temporary virtual New Zealand residents in their droves (on PlayStation, the process requires a regional account and payment in local currency so is more finicky).

In fact, according to data analytics firm Ampere Analysis, the early demand was such that 1.5m Xbox users in the US and 600,000 UK Xbox players briefly went Kiwi for the occasion of GTA 6's launch. Other countries highlighted by Ampere include Canada, where 200,000 Xbox players took the New Zealand plunge, Brazil (200,000 players), and Mexico (100,000 players).

By contrast, just 100,000 PlayStation players in the US opted to dive in early, reflecting, as Ampere notes, "the ease of being able to switch country in the account settings on Xbox consoles." And here's all that info in graph form:

Amusingly, New Zealand's tourist board tipped a wink to the sudden influx of virtual 'visitors', telling them "We'd love to have you". It also cheekily offered a video of cheerful tourists admiring the country's resplendent natural beauty "Life," read the accompanying caption, "because we're getting GTA 6 first."

Some hours later and the rest of the world can now finally, officially join in the GTA 6 fun, and it's a game worth playing. Eurogamer's Chris Tapsell called it an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in his five star GTA 6 review. And if you need some help getting through the game now it's here, you can check out Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

"There are lots of studios within EA that did that and it didn't work—they still got murdered in their sleep."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"I think the version of BioWare that survives EA better is a version where we drop down to one franchise at a time, maybe just one franchise at all. Maybe we just carve SWTOR off and they become an independent studio within EA, because I don't know how what I'm about to say makes sense if you don't do that. But you ship Mass Effect, you ship Dragon Age, and then one of those wins—I hate this—one of those wins and then you just become a one-project studio. There are lots of studios within EA that did that and it didn't work—they still got murdered in their sleep, so maybe that doesn't work anyway." Via an interview with Pembridge.

Many are asking themselves how a legendary studio like BioWare, which is responsible for staples of the PC gaming genre like Neverwinter Nights, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, and the OG Baldur's Gate, alongside Mass Effect and Dragon Age, can be shuttered.

Former Dragon Age executive producer Mark Darrah has already explained how the studio was backed into a corner by EA. Escalating financial pressure led to the poor decisions and subpar games we saw ahead of BioWare's closure. But what if it had all gone differently? Despite everything, Darrah does question whether there was a way for BioWare to survive under EA.

"BioWare's entire existence under EA—it was essentially zero sum, if somebody was getting resources it was coming at the expense of somebody else," Darrah explains. "It's almost like BioWare has run exactly the same way for its entire existence. But the external constraints were different. So in the early days when BioWare needed more people it hired more people. That's like Baldur's Gate 1, Neverwinter Nights, in the early days when we have all these different threads and branches.

"And then in 2007/2008, when the EA constraints come in, the same desires are there, we need more people to ship our games so the way we fix that in that time period is by cutting off all those other branches. So [Jade Empire sequel] Revolver goes away and the Handheld [Development] Group goes away … and so Dragon Age and Mass Effect eats everything."

The alternative? Scaling things down to meet EA's needs. "Budgets keep going up, but we're still not getting bigger… So what's happening is that the walls are closing in and we're trying to be three things [SWTOR, Mass Effect, Dragon Age] and arguably we can only afford to be two things, or one thing." There's no telling whether this would've saved BioWare, but it has worked for other studios.

"Maxis figured out how to live inside of EA and BioWare never did," Darrah adds. Focusing on just one project does seem to be the answer, or at least Darrah believes it has been for Maxis and Battlefield Studios, which both had games that initially underperformed and weren't well received. "If [Battlefield Studios] don't work on Battlefield then you might as well shut the studio down. So they all work on Battlefield 4 and they fix Battlefield 4 and it becomes successful, like very successful after the fact. The Sims 4, same thing."

On the other hand "Mass Effect Andromeda ships and then Dragon Age 4 which has been starving for resources is like 'No, no [the devs] are supposed to come to us. Where are they?' That need to keep them in place isn't there in the same way. So when I say BioWare didn't adapt to EA, that's what I mean."

#3716. Alt Video is a digital, faux Blockbuster video store that you can fill with movies from your Letterboxd watchlist and Plex server

And you can even watch those movies in-game

Since the beginning of the year, I have watched almost 150 films. I know this, because over the past few years, I've become one of those people… a Letterboxd user. Gasp! I know, I know, but I don't think I'm too insufferable about it. I'll only do a joke review in the hopes of like farming if I think it's genuinely funny! But many of these films were watched digitally, meaning I don't have a bunch of DVDs to admire on a shelf. So what am I to do? Well, I could check out Alt Video, a not quite job simulator where you can use your Letterboxd account or media server to fill up a digital, faux Blockbuster.

This is, obviously, not so dissimilar to Boxroom, a game where you can design your own bedroom that lets you use your Steam profile to fill it with games you actually own. With Alt Video, you do things slightly differently just because of the focus on a different format. So, say you have a Letterboxd account. After exporting some data from your account, you can bring that into Alt Video, and this fake video store will then get filled up with shelves of DVD cases of all the films you've watched.

Alternatively, and perhaps more enticingly, if you run something like a Plex or Jellyfin server, you can hook that up to the game too, where again all of the films you own digitally show up in store. What's more interesting here is that there's a cinema room in the store that lets you watch films on your Plex server, and it's possible to invite your Steam friends to watch along with you. There's even a few other rooms, like a '90s bedroom or family room for more of a CRT kinda vibe. It's cute! If you like you can even manually add any DVDs or Blu-rays you own to appear on all the shelves too.

There's a lot of other nice touches too. In the case of your Letterboxd data, your ratings even show up on the back of the boxes. It's not just relegated to films either, you can put in shows or even your games. The whole thing can be played in VR if you really want that immersive feel. There's a store clerk who can give you some recommendations if you're not sure what to watch. And there's even a day and night system, weather, and seasonal shopfront facelifts.

Alt Video is currently slated for release next week on November 24th, and it'll be doing so in early access. Worth noting that for now the focus is on the browsing, but features involving serving customers and running the store are on the way. You can wishlist it on Steam right here.

#3715. Ubisoft cuts jobs at major Assassin's Creed and Far Cry studios as its year of layoffs continues

Ubisoft has confirmed more layoffs as part of its previously announced operational "reset", this time affecting 166 employees at its major Montréal and Québec City studios - the teams responsible for game series including Assassin's Creed and Far Cry. It says the cuts are necessary "to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs."

GamesIndustry.biz reports the cuts - believed to equate to around four percent of the studios' total headcount - will impact employees working on projects either recently cancelled or significantly changed.

The publication also understands the cuts, said to primarily impact production and support roles at Ubisoft Montréal and Québec City, include members of Vantage Studios - Ubisoft and Tencent's joint development venture announced last October, which focuses on the publisher's biggest franchises, including Far Cry, Rainbow Six Siege, and Assassin's Creed.

In a statement provided to Eurogamer, Ubisoft confirmed it is, "reducing its workforce by 166 positions across its Montréal and Québec City operations", adding: "As our portfolio evolves, our production needs are changing, requiring us to adjust the size of some teams to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs.

"We deeply value the contributions of these teams and recognise the impact this may have on our colleagues," the statement continued. "We are committed to supporting them through this process with care and respect. Those affected are being provided with severance, extended health care benefits, career transition services and other resources."

These latest job cuts are part of a "major organisational, operational and portfolio reset" announced by Ubisoft in January. That initial announcement was accompanied by the news of two studio closures - affecting its Halifax mobile and Stockholm teams - plus the cancellation of six projects, including the much-delayed Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time remake.

Since then, 105 jobs have been cut at Red Storm Entertainment, the Ubisoft studio behind the Ghost Recon series, and around 380 employees were reportedly laid off when the publisher's Winnipeg and Belgrade teams shut in June. In October, Ubisoft closed Trials developer RedLynx and downsized its Singapore Assassin's Creed: Black Flag Resynced team, impacting a total of approximately 120 employees. Amid all this, Ubisoft developers have been on strike in response to the publisher's sweeping layoffs.
